analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans buy prescription drugs from approved Canadian pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill to let people import cheaper drugs from Canada was introduced in February 2025 with a bipartisan group of eight senators and has sat in the Senate health committee without a vote ever since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would direct the FDA to write rules letting individuals import prescription drugs from Canadian pharmacies that the FDA has vetted and listed on its website. Purchases would be limited to a 90-day personal supply with a valid US doctor's prescription, and the drug must match an FDA-approved version. The bill was referred to the Senate health committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay US prices for prescription drugs, especially people paying cash for expensive maintenance medications. Canadian prices for the same FDA-approved medicines are often far lower, and this would create a legal, vetted path to buy them directly.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to issue regulations within 180 days of enactment permitting individuals to import eligible prescription drugs from approved Canadian pharmacies.

Limits purchases to a 90-day supply for personal use, filled with a valid prescription from a US-licensed physician, and requires the drug to have the same active ingredients, dosage form, and strength as an FDA-approved drug.

Requires the FDA to certify that participating pharmacies are located and licensed in Canada, have operated for at least five years, run quality assurance programs with blind testing, and use FDA-approved laboratories for product testing, and requires the FDA to publish the list of approved pharmacies online so buyers can verify them.
Bars the riskier categories from importation, including controlled substances, biological products, intravenously injected drugs, and refrigerated drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, who would lose some of their ability to charge Americans higher prices than Canadian customers pay for identical medicines. The FDA also bears the cost of certifying and monitoring foreign pharmacies.

drawbacks.text: The bill excludes biological products and other advanced drugs, which include many of the most expensive medicines, so the people with the highest drug bills get no relief from it.
It is limited to a 90-day personal supply bought by individuals, which helps people who pay out of pocket but does not change what insurers, employers, or the health system pay overall.

The bill's own screening rules acknowledge the central risk: a supply chain outside FDA's normal oversight. It responds with pharmacy certification, laboratory testing, and quality assurance requirements, but a consumer buying from abroad relies on those checks rather than the US distribution system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is deliberately narrow, and its safety architecture is more thorough than most importation proposals, but its help is limited to individuals buying a 90-day supply of non-biologic drugs. For someone paying several hundred dollars a month out of pocket, that can be a large saving; for the drug-pricing problem as a whole, it is a small channel. The main cost is to drug manufacturers' US pricing power, which is exactly the point of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee, which has taken no action on it, so it has never come up for a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced the bill on February 19, 2025, joined by seven cosponsors including Republicans and an Independent.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off so far, because the bill has not moved and their pricing power over US consumers remains untouched. Consumers paying US drug prices are no worse off than before, but they have gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to allow personal drug importation from Canada.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the importation bill, giving it Republican support.

for.name: Sens. Baldwin, King, Merkley, Shaheen, Whitehouse, and Welch
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; King is an Independent.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has held no hearing or markup and taken no action on it.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Has consistently opposed drug importation measures that would let Americans buy identical medicines at Canadian prices.

sides.party_line_note: The eight-sponsor group spans parties: 5 of 45 Senate Democrats, 1 of 55 Senate Republicans (Grassley), and 1 of 2 Independents, though the bill has drawn no committee or floor action from either party's leadership.

industries.note: The bill opens a legal channel for Americans to buy the same FDA-approved medicines at Canadian prices, undercutting the manufacturers' ability to charge more in the US than in Canada. Because it only affects their US pricing power and does not affect public safety costs to consumers, their interest runs against the bill's beneficiaries.

Approved Canadian pharmacies would gain a new, FDA-certified stream of American customers buying a 90-day supply at a time. Their gain comes only if they pass the bill's certification and testing requirements.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and US drug middlemen
industries.note: Direct personal importation bypasses the US intermediaries who negotiate and mark up drug prices, letting consumers buy around them. The bill does not regulate them, but it offers consumers an alternative to their channel.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat untouched in the Senate HELP Committee since February 2025 with no hearing or markup. Versions of this Klobuchar-Grassley importation bill have been introduced in several prior Congresses without reaching a floor vote, and with no committee movement in this Congress, it is likely to expire the same way unless the committee schedules action.
